title: Surprise! Japanese People Come from Three Ancient Groups, Not Two
summary: Where do the Japanese people come from? Scientists used to think it was a mix of two ancient groups: the Jomon hunter-gatherers and later rice farmers from East Asia. But a giant new study just added a third group! Researchers at RIKEN in Japan read the complete DNA of more than 3,200 people from all over the country. They found evidence of a third ancestral group connected to northeast Asia, possibly the ancient Emishi people. This supports a "tripartite origins" theory—that's a fancy way of saying three-part beginnings. The study also showed something surprising: Japan isn't as genetically uniform as many thought. People in Okinawa had the most Jomon DNA (28.5%), while western Japan had much less (13.4%) and more connections to Han Chinese. The third group's DNA was strongest in the northeast. The team used whole-genome sequencing, which reads almost all 3 billion DNA letters. That's like reading every page of a huge instruction book, not just the summary. They also looked at rare gene variants that can act like ancient breadcrumbs, tracing migration routes. This discovery helps rewrite Japan's history, showing waves of people arrived over centuries. The study even found traces of Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA that still affect health today. Who knew your genes could tell such an old story?
why_it_matters: Your genes hold clues about ancient travels and mixing of different peoples, so learning about DNA can connect you to a much bigger story of human history.

background_read: For a long time, scientists believed Japan's population came from the Jomon hunter-gatherers and the Yayoi rice farmers who arrived about 2,500 years ago.
RIKEN (Japan's largest scientific research institution) carried out the biggest DNA study ever done on Japanese people, reading the complete genomes of over 3,200 volunteers.
The Emishi were a historical people of northern Honshu who resisted the early Japanese state, and their genetic legacy may now be revealed.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers at RIKEN in Japan
WHAT: Analyzed complete DNA from over 3,200 Japanese people and discovered a third ancestral group, supporting the tripartite origins theory
WHERE: Samples were collected from all over Japan, from Okinawa to the northeast
WHY: To rewrite Japan's genetic history and show that the population is made of more ancient migrations than previously thought

perspectives.description: Discovering a third ancestral group adds a new layer to Japanese heritage, showing that the country's past is even more diverse and fascinating.
Some people worry that genetic studies might be used to label or divide groups, but this research actually highlights how much mixing has happened.
This study reminds us that what we think we know can change with new evidence, and a simple two-part story isn't always the full picture.
